subject: ela
cluster: Research to build and present knowledge
description: Students conduct short research projects to answer a question, drawing on several sources and refocusing the inquiry when appropriate. They turn a broad topic into a focused, researchable question, decide what information is needed, judge whether a source is relevant and credible, pull evidence from more than one source, recognize when sources agree or conflict, and narrow or shift the question when the evidence shows the original question was too broad, too narrow, or off target. Because this is a writing and research standard, every item embeds the full question, source list, short source excerpts, notes, or planning text it depends on inside the item itself, so the student needs nothing external. Items test the components of short research through analysis, selection, and short construction rather than completing a full research paper.
subSkills: Turn a broad topic into a focused, researchable question that can be answered with evidence
Distinguish a researchable question from one that is too broad, too narrow, or a simple yes or no fact
Decide what information is needed to answer the research question and what is off topic
Judge whether a source is relevant to the research question
Judge whether a source is credible (author expertise, currency, purpose) rather than relying on a single weak source
Draw on several sources rather than one, and gather evidence from more than one source to answer the question
Recognize when two sources agree, add to each other, or conflict
Refocus or narrow the inquiry when evidence shows the question is too broad, too narrow, or pointed in the wrong direction
Organize gathered notes so they map to parts of the research question

problemArchetypes.name: Choose the focused research question
problemArchetypes.example: Read the topic and the four questions embedded in the item. 'Topic: honeybees.' Question A: 'Are honeybees insects?' Question B: 'Everything about honeybees.' Question C: 'How do honeybee colonies survive cold winters?' Question D: 'Do you like honeybees?' Which question is best for a short research project? Answer: C, because it is focused, can be answered with evidence from several sources, and is not a single yes or no fact, an opinion, or too broad to research.

problemArchetypes.name: Decide what information is needed
problemArchetypes.example: Research question embedded in the item: 'How did the printing press change how people shared news?' Which kind of information would best help answer this question? Options include a fact about the printing press's effect on news, a detail about modern printers, the inventor's birthday, and a list of paper sizes. Answer: the source about how the press changed the spread of news, because it directly answers the question while the others are off topic.

problemArchetypes.name: Judge whether a source is relevant
problemArchetypes.example: Research question in the item: 'Why are coral reefs important to ocean life?' Read the four short source descriptions embedded in the item. Which source is most relevant? Answer: the article titled 'Coral reefs as habitat for ocean species,' because it addresses the question, while a source about beach tourism or about reef-colored paint does not.

problemArchetypes.name: Judge source credibility
problemArchetypes.example: Research question in the item: 'How does sleep affect memory in students?' Read the four sources embedded in the item, including a marine biology institute report on sleep studies, a personal blog post with no author named, a snack company advertisement, and an anonymous comment. Which source is the most credible for this question? Answer: the institute report, because it has a named expert author, a clear purpose to inform, and current research, while the others lack expertise or are trying to sell something.

problemArchetypes.name: Draw on several sources
problemArchetypes.example: Read the research question and the short notes from two sources embedded in the item. Source 1 says volcanoes release ash; Source 2 says ash can affect air travel. Which statement best uses both sources to answer the question 'How can volcanic eruptions disrupt daily life?' Answer: the statement that combines ash release with its effect on air travel, because it draws on both sources rather than only one.

problemArchetypes.name: Recognize agreement or conflict between sources
problemArchetypes.example: Read the two short source excerpts embedded in the item. Source 1 states that the town festival began in 1950; Source 2 states it began in 1962. What should the researcher conclude about these sources? Answer: the sources conflict on the start date, so the researcher should look for a third, more reliable source rather than picking one at random.

problemArchetypes.name: Refocus the inquiry
problemArchetypes.example: Read the original question and the research notes embedded in the item. 'Original question: What are all the foods people eat around the world?' The student finds the topic is far too broad to cover in a short project. Which refocused question is the best next step? Answer: a narrowed question such as 'How do breakfast foods differ between Japan and the United States,' because it keeps the topic but makes it answerable in a short project.

Easy.description: A topic plus a short list of choices or a single short source description (roughly 10 to 30 words total) embedded in the item. The task is identify-level: pick the focused research question from clearly different options, choose the obviously relevant source, or name whether a question is too broad or a simple fact. Only one component of research is tested and the correct answer is unmistakable.
constraints: Stimulus is a topic with a few short question or source choices included in the prompt
Tests exactly one component (focused question, single relevant source, too broad vs researchable)
Identify-level task: select or label, no construction required
Distractors are clearly weaker (a yes or no fact, an opinion question, an obviously off-topic source)

Medium.description: A research question plus two or three short source descriptions or a brief set of notes (roughly 30 to 60 words) embedded in the item. The task is analyze-level: judge which source is most relevant or credible among plausible options, decide what information is still needed, or combine notes from two sources to answer the question. The student must weigh more than one option that is partly defensible.
constraints: Stimulus is a question with two or three short source descriptions or notes in the prompt
Tests source relevance, source credibility, drawing on several sources, or what information is needed
Analyze-level task: choose or combine based on how well a source or note answers the question
Distractors are plausible partial fits (a related but less credible source, a note that answers only part of the question)

Hard.description: A research question with two short source excerpts that agree, add to each other, or conflict, or an original question with a set of research notes (roughly 60 to 110 words) embedded in the item. The task is evaluate-level: decide how to handle conflicting sources, judge whether the gathered evidence answers the question, or choose the best refocused question when the evidence shows the original was too broad, too narrow, or off target. Requires inference about how the sources relate and where the inquiry should go next.
constraints: Stimulus is two short source excerpts or an original question with research notes included in the prompt
Tests how sources interact (agreement, conflict) and when and how to refocus the inquiry
Evaluate-level task: select the best next step, refocused question, or use of multiple sources and justify it
Requires inference to judge whether evidence answers the question and whether the inquiry should narrow, shift, or seek more sources

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student chooses a question that is too broad, mistaking a whole topic for a focused research question
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects 'Everything about honeybees' or 'All foods people eat' as the research question instead of a focused, answerable question

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student chooses a question that is a simple yes or no fact or an opinion, not a question that needs research across sources
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Picks 'Are honeybees insects?' or 'Do you like honeybees?' as the research question instead of a question requiring evidence from several sources

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats any source on the general topic as relevant, ignoring whether it actually answers the research question
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a source about beach tourism for the question 'Why are coral reefs important to ocean life?' because it mentions the ocean, not because it answers the question

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student judges a source by how interesting or easy it is rather than by credibility, accepting an ad, an anonymous post, or an off-field author
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses a snack advertisement or an unsigned blog post as the best source instead of a named expert report, because it looks appealing

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student relies on a single source instead of drawing on several, treating one source as enough to answer the question
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Picks an answer built from only one source's note when the question requires combining evidence from both provided sources

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student ignores a conflict between sources and simply picks one fact at random instead of seeking more reliable information
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses one of two conflicting dates as the final answer instead of recognizing the conflict and looking for a third reliable source

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student keeps the original question unchanged even when the evidence shows it is too broad, too narrow, or off target, refusing to refocus
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects 'keep the same broad question' instead of a refocused, narrowed question that the evidence shows is needed

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student refocuses by jumping to a completely unrelated question rather than narrowing or shifting within the same topic
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses a new question on a different topic entirely instead of a narrowed question that still answers the original inquiry
